cards.front:
What does every **physical quantity** consist of?

State · 1.1.1
cards.back:
A **numerical magnitude** and a **unit**.

Example: 9.81 m s$^{-2}$: magnitude 9.81, unit m s$^{-2}$.
Trap: a number with no unit (where one is needed) loses the mark.

cards.front:
State the **SI base quantities** and their units.

State · 1.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Mass**: kilogram (**kg**)
2. **Length**: metre (**m**)
3. **Time**: second (**s**)
4. **Current**: ampere (**A**)
5. **Temperature**: kelvin (**K**)
6. **Amount of substance**: mole (**mol**) (15.1.1)

Trap: **charge** (C), **force** (N) and **voltage** (V) are **not** base quantities: they're derived.

cards.front:
State the **prefixes** in the syllabus and their values.

State · 1.2.4

Define **systematic error** and **random error**.

Define · 1.3.1
cards.back:
1. **Systematic error**: an error of the **same size and sign** in every reading, so readings are **all too high or all too low**. It **cannot** be reduced by repeating and averaging. A **zero error** is a systematic error.
2. **Random error**: an error that makes readings **scatter about the true value** (some above, some below). It is **reduced by repeating** readings and **averaging**.

Hook: systematic shifts everything **one way**; random **scatters** both ways.

cards.front:
Distinguish between **precision** and **accuracy**.

Define · 1.3.2
cards.back:
1. **Accuracy**: how **close** a measurement (or the mean) is to the **true value**.
2. **Precision**: how **close repeated measurements are to each other** (small spread / range of readings).

Trap: readings can be **precise but not accurate** (all close together, but all off because of a systematic error).

cards.front:
Distinguish between **scalar** and **vector** quantities, with examples.

Define · 1.4.1
cards.back:
1. **Scalar**: has **magnitude only**. e.g. mass, distance, speed, time, energy, power, temperature, charge, potential.
2. **Vector**: has **magnitude and direction**. e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, electric field strength.

Trap: **work/energy** is a **scalar** even though force and displacement are vectors.

cards.front:
Define **distance** and **displacement**.

Define · 2.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Distance**: the **total length of the path** travelled. **Scalar**.
2. **Displacement**: the **distance** from a **fixed point** in a **specified direction** (straight line). **Vector**.

Example: one full lap of a 400 m track: distance 400 m, displacement **0**.

cards.front:
Define **speed** and **velocity**.

Define · 2.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Speed**: **distance travelled per unit time** (rate of change of distance). **Scalar**.
2. **Velocity**: **rate of change of displacement** (change in displacement per unit time). **Vector**.

Trap: velocity needs "**displacement**". Saying "speed in a direction" can lose the mark.

cards.front:
Define **acceleration**.

Define · 2.1.1
cards.back:
**Rate of change of velocity** (change in velocity per unit time).

$$a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ Units: m s$^{-2}$. **Vector**.
Trap: "rate of change of **speed**" is **wrong**. Circular motion at constant speed still has acceleration.

cards.front:
What is **mass**?

Define · 3.1.1
cards.back:
The **property of an object** that **resists change in motion**.

Unit: kg (base unit). **Scalar**.
Trap: mass is **not** weight. Mass doesn't change from planet to planet; weight does.

cards.front:
Define **linear momentum**.

Define · 3.1.3
cards.back:
The **product of mass and velocity**.

$$p=mv$$ Units: kg m s$^{-1}$ (= N s). **Vector**: same direction as the velocity.

cards.front:
Define **force** and the **newton**.

Define · 3.1.4
cards.back:
1. **Force**: the **rate of change of momentum**.
$$F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$
2. **1 newton**: the force that gives a **mass of 1 kg** an **acceleration of 1 m s$^{-2}$**.

$1\ \text{N}=1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$

cards.front:
State **Newton's first law** of motion.

State · 3.1.5
cards.back:
A body **remains at rest** or continues to move with **constant velocity** (constant speed in a straight line)
**unless acted on by a resultant (external) force**.

Trap: "constant **velocity**", not just constant speed.

cards.front:
State **Newton's second law** of motion.

State · 3.1.5
cards.back:
The **resultant force** on a body is **(directly) proportional to the rate of change of its momentum**,
and acts in the **direction of the change in momentum**.

$$F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ which becomes $F=ma$ for **constant mass**.
Trap: $F=ma$ is a special case. The law is about **momentum**.

cards.front:
State **Newton's third law** of motion.

State · 3.1.5
cards.back:
If body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts a force on body A that is
**equal in magnitude** and **opposite in direction** (and of the **same type**).

Trap: the two forces act on **different bodies**, so they **never cancel**. Weight and the normal reaction on a book are **not** a third-law pair.

cards.front:
What is **weight**?

Define · 3.1.6
cards.back:
The **effect of a gravitational field on a mass**: the **force** on a mass due to the gravitational field.

$$W=mg$$ Units: N. **Vector**, acting **downwards** (towards the centre of the Earth).

cards.front:
What is **terminal velocity**? When is it reached?

State · 3.2.3
cards.back:
1. The **constant (maximum) velocity** reached by an object moving against a **resistive force**.
2. It's reached when the **resistive force (drag) equals the driving force** (e.g. weight),
3. so the **resultant force is zero** and the **acceleration is zero**.

Trap: drag **increases with speed**. That's why it eventually balances the weight.

cards.front:
State the **principle of conservation of momentum**.

State · 3.3.1
cards.back:
The **total momentum** of a system **remains constant**,
provided **no resultant external force** acts on the system (an isolated system).

Trap: "**total**" and "**no external force**" are the mark points.

cards.front:
Distinguish between **elastic** and **inelastic** collisions.

Define · 3.3.3
cards.back:
1. **Elastic**: **total kinetic energy is conserved**. Also, **relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation**.
2. **Inelastic**: **kinetic energy is not conserved** (some changes to other forms, e.g. thermal).
3. In **both**: **momentum** and **total energy** are **always conserved**.

Trap: never say "energy is lost" in an elastic collision. Say **kinetic** energy is conserved.

cards.front:
Define **centre of gravity**.

Define · 4.1.1
cards.back:
The **point** through which the **(whole) weight** of an object **may be taken to act**.

For a uniform object it's at the **geometric centre**.

cards.front:
Define the **moment of a force**.

Define · 4.1.2
cards.back:
The **product** of the **force** and the **perpendicular distance** from the **pivot (point)** to the **line of action** of the force.

$$\text{moment}=F\times d_\perp$$ Units: N m.
Trap: the distance must be **perpendicular** to the force.

cards.front:
What is a **couple**?

Define · 4.1.3
cards.back:
A **pair of forces** that are **equal in magnitude**, **opposite in direction** and **parallel** but **not in the same line**,
which produce **rotation only** (no resultant force, so no translation).

cards.front:
Define the **torque of a couple**.

Define · 4.1.4
cards.back:
The **product** of **one of the forces** and the **perpendicular distance between the lines of action** of the two forces.

$$\text{torque}=F\times d$$ Units: N m.
Trap: use **one** force, not both added together.

cards.front:
State the **principle of moments**.

State · 4.2.1
cards.back:
For a body in **equilibrium**, the **sum of the clockwise moments** about **any point**
**equals** the **sum of the anticlockwise moments** about **the same point**.

cards.front:
State the two **conditions for equilibrium**.

State · 4.2.2
cards.back:
1. **No resultant force** (forces balance in every direction).
2. **No resultant torque / moment** (about any point).

Hook: no **sliding** and no **spinning**.

cards.front:
Define **density**.

Define · 4.3.1
cards.back:
**Mass per unit volume**.

$$\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$$ Units: kg m$^{-3}$.

cards.front:
Define **pressure**.

Define · 4.3.2
cards.back:
**(Normal) force per unit area** (force acting **perpendicular** to the area).

$$p=\dfrac{F}{A}$$ Units: Pa (= N m$^{-2}$). **Scalar**.

cards.front:
What is **upthrust**, and what causes it?

Define · 4.3.5
cards.back:
1. The **upward force** on an object in a **fluid**.
2. It is caused by the **difference in hydrostatic pressure** between the **top and bottom** of the object (pressure is greater lower down).
3. Upthrust = **weight of fluid displaced**: $F=\rho gV$.

$\rho$: density of the **fluid** · $V$: volume **displaced**.

cards.front:
Define **work done** and the **joule**.

Define · 5.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Work done**: the **product** of the **force** and the **displacement in the direction of the force**.
$$W=Fs\cos\theta$$
2. **1 joule**: the work done when a **force of 1 N** moves its point of application **1 m** in the **direction of the force**.

cards.front:
State the **principle of conservation of energy**.

State · 5.1.2

Define **efficiency**.

Define · 5.1.3
cards.back:
The **ratio** of the **useful energy (or power) output** to the **total energy (or power) input**.

$$\text{efficiency}=\dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\ (\times100\%)$$
No units. Always **less than 1** (100%).

cards.front:
Define **power** and the **watt**.

Define · 5.1.5
cards.back:
1. **Power**: **work done per unit time** (rate of doing work / energy transferred per unit time).
$$P=\dfrac{W}{t}$$
2. **1 watt** = **1 joule per second**.

cards.front:
What is **gravitational potential energy** and **kinetic energy**?

Define · 5.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Gravitational potential energy**: energy a mass has because of its **position in a gravitational field**. $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ (uniform field).
2. **Kinetic energy**: energy an object has because of its **motion**. $E_k=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

cards.front:
Distinguish between **tensile** and **compressive** forces.

Define · 6.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Tensile** forces **stretch** an object: they cause **extension** (positive).
2. **Compressive** forces **squash** an object: they cause **compression** (negative).

cards.front:
Define **load**, **extension**, **compression** and **limit of proportionality**.

Define · 6.1.2
cards.back:
1. **Load**: the **force** applied that causes deformation.
2. **Extension**: the **increase in length**.
3. **Compression**: the **decrease in length**.
4. **Limit of proportionality**: the point beyond which the **extension is no longer proportional to the load** (Hooke's law no longer obeyed).

cards.front:
State **Hooke's law** and define the **spring constant**.

State · 6.1.3
cards.back:
1. **Hooke's law**: the **extension** is **(directly) proportional to the force (load)** applied,
2. provided the **limit of proportionality** is **not exceeded**.
3. **Spring constant**: **force per unit extension**.
$$k=\dfrac{F}{x}$$ Units: N m$^{-1}$.

cards.front:
Define **stress**, **strain** and the **Young modulus**.

Define · 6.1.5
cards.back:
1. **Stress**: **force per unit cross-sectional area**. $\sigma=\dfrac{F}{A}$ (Pa)
2. **Strain**: **extension per unit original length**. $\varepsilon=\dfrac{x}{L}$ (**no units**)
3. **Young modulus**: **stress ÷ strain** (within the **limit of proportionality**). $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$ (Pa)

Trap: strain uses the **original** length.

cards.front:
Define **elastic deformation**, **plastic deformation** and **elastic limit**.

Define · 6.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Elastic deformation**: the material **returns to its original shape/length** when the **load is removed**.
2. **Plastic deformation**: **permanent** deformation: the material **does not return** to its original shape when the load is removed.
3. **Elastic limit**: the **maximum load** (point) beyond which the material **will not return to its original length** when the load is removed.

Trap: the elastic limit is **not** the same as the limit of proportionality (it comes at or after it).

cards.front:
What is **elastic potential (strain) energy**, and what does the area under a force–extension graph represent?

State · 6.2.2
cards.back:
1. **Elastic potential energy**: energy **stored** in a body because it is **deformed**.
2. **Area under the force–extension graph** = **work done** (energy stored).
3. Within the limit of proportionality: $E_p=\tfrac{1}{2}Fx=\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

cards.front:
What does a **progressive wave** do?

Define · 7.1.6
cards.back:
It **transfers energy** from one place to another
**without transferring matter**, by **oscillations** (of particles or of fields).

cards.front:
Define **displacement**, **amplitude** and **wavelength** for a wave.

Define · 7.1.2
cards.back:
1. **Displacement**: the **distance** of a point (particle) from its **equilibrium position** (in a given direction).
2. **Amplitude**: the **maximum displacement** from the **equilibrium position**.
3. **Wavelength**: the **distance between two adjacent points** on the wave that are **in phase** (e.g. crest to adjacent crest).

cards.front:
Define **period**, **frequency**, **wave speed** and **phase difference** for a wave.

Define · 7.1.2
cards.back:
1. **Period**: the **time for one complete oscillation** (of a point on the wave).
2. **Frequency**: the **number of oscillations per unit time**.
3. **Wave speed**: the **distance travelled by the wave (energy) per unit time**.
4. **Phase difference**: the **fraction of a cycle** between the oscillations of two points (or two waves), given in **degrees or radians**.

$v=f\lambda$, $f=\dfrac{1}{T}$

cards.front:
Define **intensity** of a wave.

Define · 7.1.7
cards.back:
**Power per unit area** (area **perpendicular** to the direction of the wave).

$$I=\dfrac{P}{A}$$ Units: W m$^{-2}$.
Also: **intensity ∝ (amplitude)$^2$**. Double the amplitude, **4×** the intensity.

cards.front:
Distinguish between **transverse** and **longitudinal** waves.

Define · 7.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Transverse**: particles oscillate **perpendicular (at 90°)** to the **direction of energy transfer** (wave travel). e.g. EM waves, waves on a string.
2. **Longitudinal**: particles oscillate **parallel** to the **direction of energy transfer**. e.g. sound. They have **compressions** and **rarefactions**.

Only **transverse** waves can be **polarised**.

cards.front:
What is the **Doppler effect** for sound?

State · 7.3.1
cards.back:
When a **source** of sound **moves relative to a (stationary) observer**, the **observed frequency is different** from the **source frequency**.
1. Source moving **towards** the observer: observed frequency **higher**.
2. Source moving **away**: observed frequency **lower**.

$$f_o=\dfrac{f_sv}{v\pm v_s}$$ ($-$ approaching, $+$ receding)
Trap: the **source** frequency doesn't change; only the **observed** one does.

cards.front:
State two properties shared by **all electromagnetic waves**.

State · 7.4.1
cards.back:
1. They are all **transverse** waves.
2. They all travel at the **same speed** $c$ in **free space (a vacuum)**: $c=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

cards.front:
State the regions of the **electromagnetic spectrum** in order, with approximate wavelengths.

State · 7.4.2
cards.back:
Shortest to longest wavelength (approx., the ranges overlap):
1. **γ-rays**: $<10^{-11}$ m
2. **X-rays**: $10^{-13}$ to $10^{-8}$ m
3. **Ultraviolet**: $10^{-8}$ to $4\times10^{-7}$ m
4. **Visible**: **400–700 nm** ($4\times10^{-7}$ to $7\times10^{-7}$ m) (7.4.3)
5. **Infrared**: $7\times10^{-7}$ to $10^{-3}$ m
6. **Microwaves**: $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$ m
7. **Radio waves**: $>10^{-1}$ m

Hook: **G**reat e**X**plorers **U**se **V**ery **I**nteresting **M**aps and **R**adios.

cards.front:
What is meant by a **plane-polarised** wave? State **Malus's law**.

Define · 7.5.1
cards.back:
1. A **plane-polarised** wave has **oscillations in one plane only** (that contains the direction of travel).
2. Polarisation only happens with **transverse** waves.
3. **Malus's law**: the transmitted intensity is $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the **plane of polarisation** of the wave and the **transmission axis** of the polariser.

Trap: Malus's law uses $\cos^{\mathbf 2}$, because intensity ∝ amplitude$^2$.

cards.front:
State the **principle of superposition**.

State · 8.1.1
cards.back: When **two (or more) waves meet** at a point, the **resultant displacement** is the **(vector) sum** of the **individual displacements**.

cards.front:
What is a **stationary wave**? Define **node** and **antinode**.

Define · 8.1.3
cards.back:
1. A **stationary wave** is formed by the **superposition** of **two waves** of the **same frequency** (and speed) travelling in **opposite directions** (often a wave and its reflection).
2. **Node**: a point of **zero amplitude**.
3. **Antinode**: a point of **maximum amplitude**.

Distance between **adjacent nodes** = $\lambda/2$.
Trap: a stationary wave **does not transfer energy**.

cards.front:
Explain the meaning of the term **diffraction**.

Define · 8.2.1
cards.back:
The **spreading** of a wave as it passes **through a gap** or **around an edge (obstacle)**.

Most noticeable when the **gap width ≈ wavelength**.
Trap: the wavelength and speed **don't change**: only the direction spreads.

cards.front:
Define **interference** and **coherence**.

Define · 8.3.1
cards.back:
1. **Interference**: the **superposition** of two (or more) **coherent** waves where they **overlap**, giving **regions of maximum and minimum** intensity (constructive and destructive).
2. **Coherence**: waves (sources) with a **constant phase difference** (so also the **same frequency**).

cards.front:
State the **conditions** needed to observe two-source **interference fringes**.

State · 8.3.3
cards.back:
1. The sources must be **coherent** (**constant phase difference**).
2. Same **frequency / wavelength** (follows from coherence).
3. Similar **amplitudes** (for clear, dark minima).
4. For transverse waves: same **plane of polarisation** (or unpolarised).

Constructive (sources in phase): path difference $=n\lambda$. Destructive: $(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$.

cards.front:
Define **electric current** and the **coulomb**.

Define · 9.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Electric current**: a **flow of charge carriers**; the **rate of flow of charge**.
$$I=\dfrac{Q}{t}$$
2. **1 coulomb**: the charge that passes a point when a **current of 1 A** flows for **1 s**. ($1\ \text{C}=1\ \text{A s}$)

cards.front:
What does it mean that **charge is quantised**?

State · 9.1.2
cards.back:
Charge only exists in **whole-number multiples** of the **elementary charge** $e$.

$e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C (the charge on a proton; an electron is $-e$).
Example: a charge of $2.4\times10^{-19}$ C is **impossible** ($1.5e$).

cards.front:
Define **potential difference** and the **volt**.

Define · 9.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Potential difference** across a component: the **energy transferred** (from electrical to other forms) **per unit charge**.
$$V=\dfrac{W}{Q}$$
2. **1 volt** = **1 joule per coulomb**.

cards.front:
Define **resistance** and the **ohm**.

Define · 9.3.1
cards.back:
1. **Resistance**: the **ratio** of the **potential difference across** a component to the **current in** it.
$$R=\dfrac{V}{I}$$
2. **1 ohm** = **1 volt per ampere**.

Trap: resistance is $V/I$ at a point, **not** the gradient of an $I$–$V$ graph.

cards.front:
State **Ohm's law**.

State · 9.3.5
cards.back:
The **current** in a (metallic) conductor is **(directly) proportional** to the **potential difference** across it,
provided the **temperature** (and other physical conditions) **remains constant**.

cards.front:
Define **resistivity**.

Define · 9.3.6
cards.back:
From $R=\dfrac{\rho L}{A}$:
$$\rho=\dfrac{RA}{L}$$
The resistivity is the **resistance × cross-sectional area ÷ length** of a sample of the material. Units: **Ω m**.

It's a property of the **material**, not of the particular wire (depends on temperature).

cards.front:
State how the resistance of an **LDR** and of an (NTC) **thermistor** changes.

State · 9.3.7
cards.back:
1. **LDR**: resistance **decreases** as **light intensity increases**.
2. **Thermistor**: resistance **decreases** as **temperature increases**.

cards.front:
Define the **electromotive force (e.m.f.)** of a source.

Define · 10.1.3
cards.back:
The **energy transferred** (from other forms to **electrical**) **per unit charge**
in **driving charge around a complete circuit**.

Units: V (= J C$^{-1}$).

cards.front:
Distinguish between **e.m.f.** and **potential difference**.

Define · 10.1.4
cards.back:
1. **E.m.f.**: energy transferred from **other forms to electrical** energy **per unit charge** (in a **source**).
2. **P.d.**: energy transferred from **electrical** energy **to other forms per unit charge** (in a **component**).

Hook: e.m.f. **gives** energy to the charge; p.d. is where the charge **gives it away**.

cards.front:
What is **internal resistance**, and what does it do to the terminal p.d.?

Define · 10.1.5
cards.back:
1. The **resistance inside** a source of e.m.f.
2. When current flows, energy is lost in it (**lost volts** $=Ir$),
3. so the **terminal p.d. is less than the e.m.f.**:
$$V=E-Ir$$

cards.front:
State **Kirchhoff's first law**. What is it a consequence of?

State · 10.2.1
cards.back:
1. The **sum of the currents entering a junction** equals the **sum of the currents leaving** it.
2. It's a consequence of **conservation of charge**.

cards.front:
State **Kirchhoff's second law**. What is it a consequence of?

State · 10.2.2
cards.back:
1. In any **closed loop** of a circuit, the **sum of the e.m.f.s** equals the **sum of the p.d.s**.
2. It's a consequence of **conservation of energy**.

cards.front:
State the **principle of the potentiometer**.

State · 10.3.2
cards.back:
1. The p.d. across a **uniform** resistance wire is **proportional to its length**.
2. At the **balance point** the **galvanometer reads zero** (no current in it),
3. so the unknown p.d. **equals** the p.d. across that **length** of wire.

Used to **compare** p.d.s (or e.m.f.s): $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}=\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}$

cards.front:
Define **proton number** and **nucleon number**. Define the **unified atomic mass unit**.

Define · 11.1.3
cards.back:
1. **Proton number** $Z$: the **number of protons** in the nucleus.
2. **Nucleon number** $A$: the **total number of protons and neutrons** in the nucleus.
3. **Unified atomic mass unit** (u): $\tfrac{1}{12}$ of the **mass of a carbon-12 atom**. $1\ \text{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg (11.1.12)

cards.front:
Define **isotopes**.

Define · 11.1.4
cards.back:
Forms of the **same element** with the **same number of protons**
but **different numbers of neutrons** in their nuclei.

Same **proton number**, different **nucleon number**.

cards.front:
What is **conserved** in nuclear processes?

State · 11.1.6
cards.back:
1. **Nucleon number**
2. **Charge** (proton number, counting electrons/positrons too)

So the top numbers and the bottom numbers both **balance** in a nuclear equation.

cards.front:
State the **composition, mass and charge** of α, β$^-$, β$^+$ and γ radiation.

State · 11.1.7
cards.back:
1. **α**: a **helium nucleus** (2 protons + 2 neutrons). Mass **4u**, charge **+2e**.
2. **β$^-$**: a fast **electron**. Mass $\approx\tfrac{1}{2000}$u, charge **−e**.
3. **β$^+$**: a fast **positron**. Mass $\approx\tfrac{1}{2000}$u, charge **+e**.
4. **γ**: **electromagnetic radiation** (photons). **No mass, no charge**.

Speeds: α slowest, β up to $\approx0.99c$, γ at $c$.

cards.front:
What is an **antiparticle**?

Define · 11.1.8
cards.back:
A particle with the **same mass** but **opposite charge** to the corresponding particle.

Example: the **positron** is the antiparticle of the **electron**.

cards.front:
Which (anti)neutrino is produced in β$^-$ and β$^+$ decay? Why do β-particles have a range of energies?

State · 11.1.9
cards.back:
1. **β$^-$ decay**: an (electron) **antineutrino** is produced.
2. **β$^+$ decay**: an (electron) **neutrino** is produced.
3. α-particles have **discrete** energies, but β-particles have a **continuous range** of energies, because the energy released is **shared** between the β-particle and the **(anti)neutrino** (11.1.10).

cards.front:
What is a **quark**? State the six flavours and their charges.

Define · 11.2.1
cards.back:
1. A quark is a **fundamental particle**.
2. Six **flavours**: **up, down, strange, charm, top, bottom**.
3. Charges: **u, c, t**: $+\tfrac{2}{3}e$. **d, s, b**: $-\tfrac{1}{3}e$.
4. Each **antiquark** has the **opposite charge**.

Hook: the "up-type" ones (u, c, t) are $+\tfrac{2}{3}$.

cards.front:
State the quark composition of a **proton** and a **neutron**.

State · 11.2.3
cards.back:
1. Protons and neutrons are **not fundamental**: they're made of quarks.
2. **Proton**: **uud** (charge $+\tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{2}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}=+1$)
3. **Neutron**: **udd** (charge $+\tfrac{2}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}=0$)

cards.front:
Define **hadron**, **baryon** and **meson**.

Define · 11.2.4
cards.back:
1. **Hadron**: a particle **made of quarks**.
2. **Baryon**: a hadron of **three quarks** (or three antiquarks). e.g. proton, neutron.
3. **Meson**: a hadron of **one quark and one antiquark**.

cards.front:
State the **quark changes** in β$^-$ and β$^+$ decay.

State · 11.2.5
cards.back:
1. **β$^-$**: a **down** quark changes to an **up** quark: $d\to u+e^-+\bar{\nu}$ (neutron → proton)
2. **β$^+$**: an **up** quark changes to a **down** quark: $u\to d+e^++\nu$ (proton → neutron)

cards.front:
What is a **lepton**?

Define · 11.2.6
cards.back:
A **fundamental particle** that is **not made of quarks**.
**Electrons** and **neutrinos** (and their antiparticles) are **leptons**.

cards.front:
Define the **radian**.

Define · A Level 12.1.1
cards.back:
The **angle subtended at the centre** of a circle by an **arc equal in length to the radius**.

$$\theta=\dfrac{s}{r}$$ $2\pi$ rad $=360^\circ$.

cards.front:
Define **angular speed**.

Define · A Level 12.1.2
cards.back:
The **rate of change of angular displacement** (angle swept out per unit time).

$$\omega=\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$$ Units: rad s$^{-1}$. Linked to speed by $v=r\omega$.

cards.front:
What causes **circular motion**? State the direction of **centripetal acceleration**.

State · A Level 12.2.1
cards.back:
1. A force of **constant magnitude** that is **always perpendicular** to the direction of motion
2. causes a **centripetal acceleration** directed **towards the centre** of the circle,
3. giving circular motion at **constant speed (angular speed)**.

$a=r\omega^2=\dfrac{v^2}{r}$
Trap: centripetal force is **not** an extra force: it's the **resultant** (e.g. tension, gravity, friction).

cards.front:
What is a **gravitational field**? Define **gravitational field strength**.

Define · A Level 13.1.1
cards.back:
1. A **gravitational field** is a **region** where a **mass** experiences a **force** (a field of force).
2. **Gravitational field strength**: the **force per unit mass**.
$$g=\dfrac{F}{m}$$ Units: N kg$^{-1}$. **Vector**.

cards.front:
For a point outside a uniform sphere, how can its mass be treated?

State · A Level 13.2.1
cards.back:
As a **point mass at its centre**.

So $r$ is measured from the **centre**: $r=R+h$.

cards.front:
State **Newton's law of gravitation**.

State · A Level 13.2.2
cards.back:
The (attractive) force between two **point masses** is **proportional to the product of their masses**
and **inversely proportional to the square of their separation**.

$$F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$

cards.front:
State the properties of a **geostationary orbit**.

State · A Level 13.2.4
cards.back:
1. **Period = 24 hours**.
2. **Directly above the Equator** (equatorial orbit).
3. Moves **west to east** (same direction as the Earth's rotation).
4. So it **remains above the same point** on the Earth's surface.

cards.front:
Define **gravitational potential** at a point.

Define · A Level 13.4.1
cards.back:
The **work done per unit mass** in bringing a **small test mass** **from infinity** to that point.

$$\phi=-\dfrac{GM}{r}$$ Units: J kg$^{-1}$. **Scalar**, always **negative**.

cards.front:
Define the **gravitational potential energy** of a mass at a point.

Define · A Level 13.4.3
cards.back:
The **work done** in bringing the mass **from infinity** to that point.

$$E_p=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$$ Units: J. **Scalar**.

cards.front:
Which way does thermal energy flow? Define **thermal equilibrium**.

State · A Level 14.1.1
cards.back:
1. (Thermal) energy is transferred from a region of **higher temperature** to a region of **lower temperature**.
2. **Thermal equilibrium**: regions at the **same temperature**, so there is **no net transfer of thermal energy** between them.

cards.front:
What is a **thermometric property**? How is the **thermodynamic scale** different?

State · A Level 14.2.1
cards.back:
1. A **physical property that varies with temperature** can be used to measure temperature. e.g. volume of a liquid, resistance of a metal, e.m.f. of a thermocouple.
2. The **thermodynamic (kelvin) scale** does **not depend on the property of any particular substance** (14.2.2).

cards.front:
What is **absolute zero**? How do you convert between °C and K?

Define · A Level 14.2.4
cards.back:
1. The **lowest possible temperature**: **zero kelvin** on the thermodynamic scale.
2. At absolute zero a substance has **minimum internal energy**.
3. $$T/\text{K}=\theta/^\circ\text{C}+273.15$$

Trap: a temperature **difference** of 1 K equals a difference of 1 °C.

cards.front:
Define **specific heat capacity**.

Define · A Level 14.3.1
cards.back:
The **energy required per unit mass** to **raise the temperature by one degree** (1 K).

$$c=\dfrac{E}{m\Delta\theta}$$ Units: J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

cards.front:
Define **specific latent heat**. Distinguish fusion and vaporisation.

Define · A Level 14.3.2
cards.back:
1. **Specific latent heat**: the **energy required per unit mass** to **change the state** of a substance **without a change in temperature**.
$$L=\dfrac{E}{m}$$ Units: J kg$^{-1}$.
2. **Fusion**: **solid ↔ liquid** (melting).
3. **Vaporisation**: **liquid ↔ gas** (boiling).

Vaporisation is bigger: molecules must be separated **much further** and work is done **pushing back the atmosphere**.

cards.front:
What is the **mole** and the **Avogadro constant**?

Define · A Level 15.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Amount of substance** is an **SI base quantity** with base unit the **mole (mol)**.
2. **One mole** contains $N_A$ particles.
3. **Avogadro constant** $N_A=6.02\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$: the **number of particles per mole**.

cards.front:
What is an **ideal gas**?

Define · A Level 15.2.1
cards.back:
A gas that obeys $pV\propto T$ (i.e. $pV=nRT$) at **all pressures, volumes and temperatures**,
where $T$ is the **thermodynamic temperature**.

Trap: $T$ must be in **kelvin**.

cards.front:
State the **basic assumptions of the kinetic theory** of gases.

State · A Level 15.3.1
cards.back:
1. A gas has a **very large number** of molecules in **continuous random motion**.
2. **Intermolecular forces are negligible** (except during collisions).
3. The **volume of the molecules is negligible** compared with the **volume of the gas (container)**.
4. **Collisions are elastic** (with each other and the walls).
5. The **time of a collision is negligible** compared with the **time between collisions**.

Hook: tiny, fast, random, bouncy, no sticking.

cards.front:
Define the **Boltzmann constant**. State the **mean kinetic energy** of a gas molecule.

State · A Level 15.2.3
cards.back:
1. $$k=\dfrac{R}{N_A}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$$
2. Average translational **kinetic energy** of a molecule:
$$\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle c^2\rangle=\tfrac{3}{2}kT$$
3. So mean kinetic energy is **proportional to the thermodynamic temperature** (15.3.4).

cards.front:
Define **internal energy**.

Define · A Level 16.1.1
cards.back:
The **sum** of a **random distribution** of the **kinetic and potential energies** of the **molecules** in a system.

It's determined by the **state** of the system.
A **rise in temperature** means an **increase in internal energy** (16.1.2).
Ideal gas: **no potential energy**, so internal energy = total kinetic energy.

cards.front:
State the **first law of thermodynamics**.

State · A Level 16.2.2
cards.back:
The **increase in internal energy** of a system equals the **thermal energy supplied to** the system (heating) **plus** the **work done on** the system.

$$\Delta U=q+W$$
Trap: $W$ is work done **on** the gas. If the gas **expands**, it does work, so $W$ is **negative**.

cards.front:
Define **displacement**, **amplitude**, **period** and **frequency** for an oscillation.

Define · A Level 17.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Displacement**: distance from the **equilibrium position** (in a given direction).
2. **Amplitude**: **maximum displacement** from the equilibrium position.
3. **Period**: **time for one complete oscillation**.
4. **Frequency**: **number of oscillations per unit time**.

cards.front:
Define **angular frequency** and **phase difference**.

Define · A Level 17.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Angular frequency**: $\omega=2\pi f=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ (the rate of change of phase angle). Units: rad s$^{-1}$.
2. **Phase difference**: the **fraction of a cycle** between two oscillations, in **degrees or radians**.

cards.front:
Define **simple harmonic motion**.

Define · A Level 17.1.2
cards.back:
Motion in which the **acceleration** is **(directly) proportional to the displacement** from a **fixed point**
and is **directed towards** that point (opposite to the displacement).

$$a=-\omega^2x$$

cards.front:
What is **damping**?

Define · A Level 17.3.1
cards.back:
The **loss of energy** (and decrease in **amplitude**) of an oscillating system
caused by a **resistive force** that **opposes the motion**.

cards.front:
Define **light**, **critical** and **heavy** damping.

Define · A Level 17.3.2
cards.back:
1. **Light**: the system **oscillates** with **gradually decreasing amplitude**.
2. **Critical**: returns to **equilibrium** in the **shortest possible time** **without oscillating**.
3. **Heavy**: returns to equilibrium **without oscillating**, but **slowly** (longer than critical).

cards.front:
Define **natural frequency**, **forced oscillation** and **resonance**.

Define · A Level 17.3.3
cards.back:
1. **Natural frequency**: the frequency at which a system **oscillates freely** (no driving force).
2. **Forced oscillation**: oscillation caused by an **external periodic driving force**.
3. **Resonance**: **maximum amplitude** of oscillation, when the **driving frequency equals the natural frequency**.

cards.front:
What is an **electric field**? Define **electric field strength**.

Define · A Level 18.1.1
cards.back:
1. An **electric field** is a **region** where a **charge** experiences a **force** (a field of force).
2. **Electric field strength**: the **force per unit positive charge**.
$$E=\dfrac{F}{q}$$ Units: N C$^{-1}$ (= V m$^{-1}$). **Vector**.

cards.front:
For a point outside a spherical conductor, how can its charge be treated?

State · A Level 18.3.1
cards.back:
As a **point charge at its centre**.

So $r$ is measured from the **centre** of the sphere.

cards.front:
State **Coulomb's law**.

State · A Level 18.3.2
cards.back:
The force between two **point charges** is **proportional to the product of the charges**
and **inversely proportional to the square of their separation**.

$$F=\dfrac{Q_1Q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$$

cards.front:
Define **electric potential** at a point.

Define · A Level 18.5.1
cards.back:
The **work done per unit positive charge** in bringing a **small test charge** **from infinity** to that point.

$$V=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$$ Units: V. **Scalar**.

cards.front:
State the relationship between **electric field strength** and **potential**.

State · A Level 18.5.2
cards.back:
The **electric field strength** at a point equals the **negative of the potential gradient** at that point.

$$E=-\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}$$

cards.front:
Define the **electric potential energy** of a charge at a point.

Define · A Level 18.5.4
cards.back:
The **work done** in bringing the charge **from infinity** to that point.

$$E_p=\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$$ Units: J. **Scalar**.

cards.front:
Define **capacitance** (isolated sphere and parallel plates) and the **farad**.

Define · A Level 19.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Capacitance**: the **charge stored per unit potential** (difference).
$$C=\dfrac{Q}{V}$$
2. **Isolated sphere**: $Q$ = charge on the sphere, $V$ = **potential** of the sphere.
3. **Parallel plates**: $Q$ = charge on **one plate**, $V$ = **p.d. between** the plates.
4. **1 farad** = **1 coulomb per volt**.

cards.front:
What is the **time constant** of a capacitor discharging through a resistor?

Define · A Level 19.3.2
cards.back:
1. $$\tau=RC$$ Units: s.
2. It is the **time taken** for the charge (or current, or p.d.) to fall to $\dfrac{1}{e}$ (**≈ 37%**) of its **initial value**.

cards.front:
What is a **magnetic field**? What produces it?

Define · A Level 20.1.1
cards.back:
1. A **region** where a **magnetic pole**, a **moving charge** or a **current-carrying conductor** experiences a **force** (a field of force).
2. Produced by **moving charges** (currents) or **permanent magnets**.
3. The field of a **solenoid** is **increased by a ferrous (iron) core** (20.4.2).

cards.front:
Define **magnetic flux density** and the **tesla**.

Define · A Level 20.2.3
cards.back:
1. **Magnetic flux density**: the **force per unit current per unit length** on a wire placed **at right angles** to the magnetic field.
$$B=\dfrac{F}{IL}$$
2. **1 tesla**: the flux density that gives a **force of 1 N** on a wire of **length 1 m** carrying **1 A** **at right angles** to the field.

cards.front:
Define **magnetic flux** and the **weber**.

Define · A Level 20.5.1
cards.back:
1. **Magnetic flux**: the **product** of the **magnetic flux density** and the **cross-sectional area perpendicular** to the field.
$$\Phi=BA$$
2. **1 weber** = **1 T m$^2$**.

cards.front:
Define **magnetic flux linkage**.

Define · A Level 20.5.3
cards.back:
The **product** of the **number of turns** of a coil and the **magnetic flux** through it.

$$\text{flux linkage}=N\Phi$$ Units: Wb (or Wb-turns).

cards.front:
State **Faraday's law** of electromagnetic induction.

State · A Level 20.5.5
cards.back:
The **induced e.m.f.** is **(directly) proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage**.

$$E=-\dfrac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$

cards.front:
State **Lenz's law**.

State · A Level 20.5.5
cards.back:
The **direction** of the **induced e.m.f.** (or current) is such that it **opposes the change** (in flux) that **produces** it.

It's a consequence of **conservation of energy**. It gives the **minus sign** in Faraday's law.

cards.front:
Define **period**, **frequency** and **peak value** of an alternating current.

Define · A Level 21.1.1
cards.back:
1. **Period**: the **time for one complete cycle**.
2. **Frequency**: the **number of cycles per unit time**.
3. **Peak value**: the **maximum** value of the current (or voltage) from zero.

cards.front:
Define the **root-mean-square (r.m.s.)** value of an alternating current.

Define · A Level 21.1.4
cards.back:
The value of the **direct current** that would **dissipate the same (mean) power** in a **resistor** as the alternating current.

Sinusoidal: $$I_{\text{r.m.s.}}=\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$$
Mean power in a resistor = **half** the maximum power (21.1.3).

cards.front:
What is **rectification**? Distinguish half-wave and full-wave.

Define · A Level 21.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Rectification**: converting **alternating current** into **direct current** (current in one direction only).
2. **Half-wave**: only **one half** of each cycle passes; the other half is **zero**.
3. **Full-wave**: **both halves** pass, with the negative half **flipped** to positive.

cards.front:
What is a **photon**? State its energy and momentum.

Define · A Level 22.1.2
cards.back:
1. A **photon** is a **quantum** (discrete packet) of **electromagnetic energy**.
2. Energy: $E=hf$
3. Momentum: $p=\dfrac{E}{c}$ (22.1.5)

cards.front:
What is the **photoelectric effect**?

Define · A Level 22.2.1
cards.back: The **emission of electrons** from a **metal surface** when it is **illuminated by electromagnetic radiation** (of high enough frequency).

cards.front:
Define **threshold frequency**, **threshold wavelength** and **work function**.

Define · A Level 22.2.2
cards.back:
1. **Threshold frequency**: the **minimum frequency** of EM radiation that causes **emission of electrons** from the surface.
2. **Threshold wavelength**: the **maximum wavelength** that causes emission.
3. **Work function**: the **minimum energy** needed to **remove an electron** from the **surface** of the metal (22.2.3).

$$hf=\Phi+\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2$$

cards.front:
State the evidence for **wave–particle duality**.

State · A Level 22.3.1
cards.back:
1. **Photoelectric effect**: evidence for the **particle** nature of **EM radiation**.
2. **Interference and diffraction**: evidence for the **wave** nature of **EM radiation**.
3. **Electron diffraction**: evidence for the **wave** nature of **particles** (22.3.2).

cards.front:
What is the **de Broglie wavelength**?

Define · A Level 22.3.3
cards.back:
The **wavelength associated with a moving particle**.

$$\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{mv}$$

cards.front:
What are **energy levels**? Define **emission** and **absorption line spectra**.

State · A Level 22.4.1
cards.back:
1. Electrons in **isolated atoms** can only have certain **discrete energies** (energy levels).
2. When an electron moves between levels, a **photon** is emitted or absorbed: $hf=E_1-E_2$.
3. **Emission line spectrum**: **bright lines** on a dark background (electrons **dropping** down levels).
4. **Absorption line spectrum**: **dark lines** on a continuous spectrum (photons **absorbed** as electrons move up).

cards.front:
State the **mass–energy equivalence**.

State · A Level 23.1.1
cards.back:
**Mass and energy are equivalent**: a change in energy means a change in mass.

$$E=mc^2$$ ($\Delta E=c^2\Delta m$)

cards.front:
Define **mass defect** and **binding energy**.

Define · A Level 23.1.3
cards.back:
1. **Mass defect**: the **difference** between the **total mass of the separate nucleons** and the **mass of the nucleus**.
2. **Binding energy**: the **energy required to separate** a nucleus into its **individual nucleons** (to infinity).

Binding energy $=\Delta m\,c^2$. Higher **binding energy per nucleon** = more **stable** (peak near iron-56).

cards.front:
Explain what is meant by **nuclear fusion** and **nuclear fission**.

Define · A Level 23.1.5
cards.back:
1. **Fusion**: **two light nuclei** **combine** to form a **heavier nucleus**, releasing energy.
2. **Fission**: a **heavy nucleus** **splits** into **two lighter nuclei** of similar mass (plus neutrons), releasing energy.

Both release energy because **binding energy per nucleon increases**.

cards.front:
What is meant by radioactive decay being **spontaneous** and **random**?

Define · A Level 23.2.2
cards.back:
1. **Spontaneous**: **not affected by external factors** (temperature, pressure, chemical state).
2. **Random**: it **cannot be predicted** **which** nucleus will decay or **when**; each nucleus has a **constant probability** of decay per unit time.
3. Evidence for randomness: **fluctuations in count rate** (23.2.1).

cards.front:
Define **activity** and **decay constant**.

Define · A Level 23.2.3
cards.back:
1. **Activity**: the **number of nuclear decays per unit time**. Units: Bq (1 Bq = 1 decay s$^{-1}$).
2. **Decay constant**: the **probability** that a nucleus will **decay per unit time**. Units: s$^{-1}$.
$$A=\lambda N$$

cards.front:
Define **half-life**.

Define · A Level 23.2.4
cards.back:
The **time taken** for the **number of undecayed nuclei** (of a particular isotope) to **fall to half** its initial value.

$$t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}{\lambda}$$
Trap: say "**undecayed nuclei**", not "the mass" or "the substance".

cards.front:
What is the **piezo-electric effect**? What is **ultrasound**?

Define · A Level 24.1.1
cards.back:
1. A **piezo-electric crystal** **changes shape** when a **p.d. is applied** across it,
2. and **generates an e.m.f.** when its **shape changes**.
3. **Ultrasound**: sound with a **frequency above 20 kHz** (above human hearing).

cards.front:
Define **specific acoustic impedance**.

Define · A Level 24.1.4
cards.back:
The **product** of the **density** of a medium and the **speed of sound** in it.

$$Z=\rho c$$ Units: kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.
A **big difference** in $Z$ at a boundary means **more reflection**.

cards.front:
What is **attenuation**?

Define · A Level 24.1.6
cards.back:
The **decrease in intensity** of a beam (ultrasound or X-rays) as it passes through matter.

$$I=I_0e^{-\mu x}$$ $\mu$: **(linear) attenuation (absorption) coefficient** (m$^{-1}$) · $x$: thickness (m).

cards.front:
What is meant by **contrast** in X-ray imaging?

Define · A Level 24.2.2
cards.back:
The **difference in the degree of blackening** between **different areas** (tissues) of the image.

Good contrast: tissues with **very different attenuation** (e.g. bone and soft tissue). Improved with a **contrast medium** (e.g. barium).

cards.front:
What is **CT scanning**?

State · A Level 24.2.4
cards.back:
**Computed tomography** produces a **3D image** of an internal structure
by combining **many X-ray images** of **cross-sections (slices)** taken from **different angles**.

cards.front:
What is a **tracer**? What type is used in **PET scanning**?

Define · A Level 24.3.1
cards.back:
1. A **tracer** is a substance containing **radioactive nuclei** that is **introduced into the body** and **absorbed by the tissue** being studied.
2. **PET** uses a tracer that decays by **β$^+$ decay** (emits **positrons**) (24.3.2).

cards.front:
What is **annihilation**?

Define · A Level 24.3.3
cards.back:
1. When a **particle** interacts with its **antiparticle**, they **annihilate**.
2. **Mass–energy is conserved**: their mass (and kinetic energy) becomes **energy** as **two γ-ray photons**.
3. In PET the two photons travel in **opposite directions** (conserving momentum) and are detected **outside the body** (24.3.6).

cards.front:
Define **luminosity** of a star.

Define · A Level 25.1.1
cards.back:
The **total power** of **radiation** emitted by a star.

Units: W.

cards.front:
Define **radiant flux intensity**.

Define · A Level 25.1.2
cards.back:
The **radiant power** passing **normally through unit area** (at a distance from the source).

$$F=\dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$$ Units: W m$^{-2}$. Obeys an **inverse square law**.

cards.front:
What is a **standard candle**?

Define · A Level 25.1.3
cards.back:
An astronomical object of **known luminosity**.

Measure its radiant flux intensity, then use $F=\dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$ to find its **distance**.
e.g. **Cepheid variable stars**, **type 1a supernovae**.

cards.front:
State **Wien's displacement law** and the **Stefan–Boltzmann law**.

State · A Level 25.2.1
cards.back:
1. **Wien's law**: the wavelength of **peak** emission is **inversely proportional** to the **thermodynamic temperature** of the surface.
$$\lambda_{\max}\propto\dfrac{1}{T}$$
2. **Stefan–Boltzmann law**: luminosity is proportional to **surface area** × $T^4$.
$$L=4\pi\sigma r^2T^4$$ (25.2.2)

cards.front:
What is **redshift**?

Define · A Level 25.3.1
cards.back:
An **increase in the observed wavelength** (decrease in frequency) of EM radiation from a source **moving away** from the observer.

$$\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}\approx\dfrac{\Delta f}{f}\approx\dfrac{v}{c}$$
Spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted to **longer** wavelengths.

cards.front:
State **Hubble's law**. What does it lead to?

State · A Level 25.3.4
cards.back:
1. The **recession speed** of a galaxy is **(approximately) proportional** to its **distance** from the Earth.
$$v\approx H_0d$$
2. So the **Universe is expanding**, which leads to the **Big Bang theory**: the Universe began from a **single point** (very hot and dense) and has been **expanding ever since**.
